title: The lived year close
hookLine: a year of gurpurabs, lived and not only learned
tomorrow: back to the very first words. do they sound the same now?

lines: OPEN A CALENDAR, TYPE THE DATES.
cards: Planning next year sounds simple: open a calendar, type in the dates, set reminders. Then two families at the same gurdwara compare phones, and the same gurpurab sits on different days. Nobody made a typo.
So before anything gets planned, there's a real question to settle: whose dates?

teach.b: First, look back at what this stretch has lived: Vaisakhi at the kitchen table, a dawn round, a swept road, a cold cup, lamps at the door, a backyard field day, a story told gently, a hall of mixed chairs, a month opened with a verse.
Now the planning runs into a real Sikh conversation.
Some Sikhs follow the Nanakshahi calendar, a solar calendar with fixed dates, so a gurpurab lands on the same day every year.

teach.h: OLDER DATES: SET BY THE MOON.
teach.b: Others keep the older calendar's dates, set partly by the moon, so Guru Nanak's gurpurab comes with the full moon of Katak and moves from year to year. Here's each side at its best.
Fixed dates: a Sikh calendar of its own, easy to plan around school and work, the same for everyone everywhere.
The older dates: continuity, the days kept the way earlier generations kept them, Guru Nanak's light marked by Katak's full moon. Both sides keep the same gurpurabs; they disagree about the day.
And both can stand on Guru Arjan's line from the Barah Maha: the days are blessed for those on whom grace falls.

teach.h: A DATE HOLDS THE DAY OPEN.
teach.b: A date only holds a day open.
Living it is what fills it.

how: Sikh families plan the year's gurpurabs from their gurdwara's calendar; some gurdwaras follow the Nanakshahi solar calendar and others the older lunar-solar dates, so a gurpurab can fall on different days in different places.

games.q: what does “the lived year close” mean?
o: a closing ceremony held when a gurdwara year ends
a year of gurpurabs looked back on, lived not just read
the last chapter of a full Guru Granth Sahib reading

games.q: two calendars, one year — tap the pairs.
p: dates set partly by the moon
Guru Nanak's gurpurab, in the older dates

s: every gurdwara keeps every gurpurab on the same date
some follow the Nanakshahi calendar, some the older dates, so a gurpurab can land on different days.
the Nanakshahi calendar gives gurpurabs fixed solar dates
the same day each year, easy to plan around school and work.
Guru Arjan says the date itself makes a day blessed
the days are blessed for those on whom grace falls.

games.q: you've always used fixed Nanakshahi dates. your uncle keeps the older, moon-set dates. state his best case.
o: continuity: the days kept as earlier generations kept them, with Guru Nanak's light on Katak's full moon.
the moon makes a day holier, so only lunar dates really count.
fixed dates are new, and anything new can't really be Sikh.
games.why: his best case is continuity, not magic. yours is a calendar of its own, fixed and shared. both keep the same gurpurabs, and the Barah Maha says grace, not the date, blesses the day.

practice: Count on your fingers the days of the Sikh year you've lived, not just read about: a langar you ate, a procession you saw, a lamp you lit, a story you told. One finger, one breath, for each.
If you run out of days, keep counting with the ones you'd like to live next year.

wordCard.voice: The lived year close. A year of gurpurabs looked back on, lived and not only learned, and the plan for the next one.

orig.note: Punjabi: a Guru's day; purab is a festival or holy day.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: lived, not just learned, whichever calendar is on the fridge. That's the stretch, done.
